slides.title: The Auction House Narrative
slides.alt: Flow diagram. A customer, who has a job to get done, asks auction house A, which receives the job request. Auction house A and the outcomes sit in a frame labelled Ecosystem of auction houses. If A can handle the job, an arrow labelled no need to share leads to A handles the job, all credit to A. If A cannot handle it, an arrow leads to A auctions off the job request, where B, C and others bid; an arrow labelled B wins leads to B handles the job, credit shared by A and B. Under the frame: Common goal: as many served customers as possible.
slides.notes:
• To get their jobs handled, customers ask an auction house
• If the auction house can handle the job itself, it keeps all the credit and involves no one else
• If it cannot, it can still hope for part of the credit by auctioning off the job request to the other auction houses
• The ecosystem of auction houses shares one goal: to serve as many customers as possible
• That is why the auction houses of the six groups must interoperate

slides.title: Enabling Event-Based Interactions
slides.alt: An empty area where the next slides show two graphs.
slides.notes:
• This week: two implementations of event-based interaction, one with W3C WebSub and one with MQTT (see Lecture 8)
• A first step towards an open and decentralized marketplace, in which each group operates its own auction house
• The task force designs the event ecosystem: the components that the applications of all six groups need to reach, e.g. WebSub hubs and MQTT brokers

slides.title: Enabling Event-Based Interactions
slides.alt: W3C WebSub: Groups 1, 2 and 3 are linked with each other in both directions, and each points to a resource directory, which holds a resource list of auction URLs such as http://group1.ex.org/auctions/. The right half of the slide is empty.
slides.notes:
• W3C WebSub: a brokered publish/subscribe protocol for observing resources on the open Web, at Web scale
• E.g. observe the auction houses of the other groups to be notified when they launch new auctions

slides.title: Enabling Event-Based Interactions
slides.alt: Two graphs side by side. W3C WebSub: Groups 1, 2 and 3 are linked with each other in both directions, and each points to a resource directory, which holds a resource list of auction URLs such as http://group1.ex.org/auctions/. MQTT: Groups 1, 2 and 3 are each linked in both directions to one event broker in the middle.
slides.notes:
• MQTT: a brokered publish/subscribe protocol to publish and receive events in the auction domain
• Unlike WebSub, MQTT does not emphasize openness and scalability; it is designed to be lightweight
• Keep the broker addresses in your configuration, so that your application follows whichever brokers the task force agrees on
• Task 5 compares both implementations, with measurements from the testing infrastructure of Exercise 7

slides.title: Who Operates an Instance?
slides.alt: Deployment diagram with one frame per operator. Top row: Google and Switchboard each run a WebSub hub, HiveMQ runs an MQTT broker, and the course runs the resource directory on its resource VM. Bottom row: Group 2 runs a PITAS app and an MQTT broker on its VM and a second MQTT broker on an extra VM; Group 5 runs a PITAS app on its VM.
slides.lead:
Rule 1: count operators, not machines.
A group operates its group VM and any extra VM the course gives it.
slides.notes:
• The operator of an instance is the party that decides what runs on it and can stop it
• Top row: the outside providers Google, Switchboard, HiveMQ and the course
• Bottom row: two of the six groups
• The task force repository lists four resource VMs; a group can claim one of them without asking the tutors
• Only groups that need more than these four, e.g. to host services for other groups, ask the tutors

slides.title: Your Group and the Task Force Iterate
slides.alt: Loop diagram in two frames. Frame Your group: Argue for your role (arguments and demonstrators) and Implement (WebSub, MQTT, and your own ADRs). Frame Task force: Negotiate (delegates of all six groups) and Decide (one ADR per decision in the decision log). • Your delegate needs your support: arguments and demonstrators that strengthen their position in the negotiations

slides.title: How Decisions Become Deployments
slides.lead: The [task force repository](https://github.com/unisg-scs-asse/pitas-hs26-itf/tree/main/infrastructure) contains an infrastructure-as-code setup for the resource VMs.
slides.alt: Architecture of configuration-based infrastructure-as-code tools. User input data goes into an application of templates and code files, which a runtime parses and interprets. The interpreter invokes configuration units, third-party and built-in, which read and update the system state of the infrastructure: servers, routers and switches. Configuration units are assembled into programs. Bottom line: the user initializes the IaC program, which is parsed by the runtime interpreter, which invokes configuration units, which interact with the system.
slides.source: Drosos, Sotiropoulos, Alexopoulos, Mitropoulos, Su. *When Your Infrastructure Is a Buggy Program: Understanding Faults in Infrastructure as Code Ecosystems*, Fig. 1, cropped. [PACMPL 8 (OOPSLA2), 2024](https://doi.org/10.1145/3689799), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
slides.notes:
• Data: group_vars, tfvars, secrets
• Program: site.yml, roles, main.tf
• Interpreter: ansible-playbook, tofu (GitHub Actions)
• Units: Ansible modules, OpenTofu resources
• System: resource VMs

• Infrastructure as code (IaC) is a best practice in DevOps
• More importantly, it gives all participants a standardized means to understand the current state of the infrastructure
• Executable documentation
• Since IaC is a best practice, coding agents should be good at interpreting it, too
